I have read the book 'Scarlett' by Margaret Mitchell several times and the first time I saw the movie I'm sorry to say that I was disappointed. The movie did not follow the book and made many changes that I did not like. One of the changes that I did not like the way that Lord Charles Ashley was portrayed. It made no sense to make him out to be a bad person. The way that things ended between Lord Charles Ashley and Scarlett was a lot different and the whole relationship was less intimate. Also, there was not a lot of confrontation between Scarlett and Rhett in the movie that was originally written in the book. The movie sent the two in almost completely opposite ways and they did not seem to cross paths often enough to make it seem like they still could be together in the future. A fine movie, but I believe that the movie would have been a lot better overall, had it followed the story that was written in the book

I have no idea how accurate the portrayal of Flynn is in this film but even as a work of fiction it is one of the worst films I have ever seen. The script is all over the place and leaves you wondering how they got from one scene to the next - you are only given the bare minimum information needed to follow the continuity and understand the current situation. This makes it difficult to understand Flynn's and other characters' motives and reasons for their behaviour. Add to that a lot of unrealistic and implausible situations and a story line that comes across like one of your friends is trying to tell you while you are asleep, but when you wake up and you try to remember it, it is jumbled, disjointed and completely nonsensical. There are many long and pointless musical sections in the film which to me are either poor direction or just the director experimenting and trying to be artistic. None of the characters are even remotely believable and the Flynn character comes across as a self serving liar, con man, thief, thief, murderer, bear fist fighter, gigolo and impostor who will do anything and lie to anyone to further his own dreams, yet somehow, despite his flaws, great opportunities always seem to miraculously fall into his lap. This film is not entertaining nor informative in any way and if it is not even remotely accurate then it is even more useless. To rub salt in the wound, the DVD is one of the worst transfers I have ever seen - it is not even in high definition or Dolby 5.1 - it is a telecine with scratches and many scratches. It looks like this is a film print that has been gathering dust in storage somewhere.

Creakiness and atmosphere this film has, but so unfortunately does the print I just viewed. Raymond Massey provides a laid back Sherlock Holmes, almost comically so in early scenes in his bathrobe, which he trades in for a laborer's garb to investigate the creepy mansion of Dr. Rylott (Lyn Harding). What wasn't clear to me was why Rylott would have wanted his stepdaughters dead. If as in the case of Helen (Angela Baddeley), he didn't want her to run off to get married, he would have accomplished the same thing by having her dispatched. Other curiosities abound as well. After setting an early wedding date with Helen, the fiancée is no longer heard from for the rest of the picture. The presence of a band of gypsies at the time of Violet Stoner's death provides merely a diversion, and what could have been an interesting murder tool, a poisonous snake, is diluted by the fact that it was not a cobra, the musical renderings of the Indian man servant notwithstanding. Athole Stewart competently portrays Holmes' aide Dr. Watson, though he takes some getting used to if Nigel Bruce is more your cup of tea. As Rylott, Lyn Harding is sufficiently menacing, a trait that would be put to good use as Holmes' nemesis Professor Moriarty in two later films - 1935's "The Triumph of Sherlock Holmes" and 1937's "Murder at the Baskervilles". With repeated choppiness and an unsteady camera, it's surprising that the story line isn't more disrupted than it is. It's integrity is generally maintained, even if one stretches a bit to fill in the gaps. I guess that would be my main complaint with the film, as mentally bridging some of the jump cuts in the picture proved to be a real pain in the asp.

This somewhat odd and somewhat curious film has not aged so unfortunately over the years since last viewed. Nigel Bruce provides a rather eccentric Sherlock Holmes, almost comically so in some scenes. In my case, it's rather odd for a man in such garb to enter the creepy mansion of Dr. Rylott (Lyn Harding). What was most puzzling to me was why Rylott would have kidnapped his stepdaughters. Surely, especially in the case of Mary (Angela Mar'cell), he would have expected her to run off to get married, which would have accomplished the heist by having her killed. Other curiosities abound as well. There is an inexplicable date with Holmes, whose fiancée is no longer heard from for the remainder of the film. The appearance of a band of gypsies on the scene of Miss Stoner's death is merely a diversion to show what could have been. The murder weapon, a poisonous snake, is interesting in the fact that it's not a real snake, the artistic renderings of the old man servant notwithstanding. W.G. Stewart competently plays Holmes' aide Dr. Watson, and he can certainly be used even if Nigel Bruce is not your cup of tea. As Rylott, Lyn Harding is sufficiently menacing, a trait that would be put to good use as Holmes' nemesis Professor Moriarty in two later films - 1930's "The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes" and 1939's "Murder at the Baskervilles". With repeated appearances of Holmes and an inexplicable date, it's surprising that the story line isn't more disrupted than it is. The overall integrity is still maintained, even if one stretches a bit to fill in the gaps. I suppose that would be my only complaint with the film, as sorting out some of the various elements in the picture proved to be a real pain in the asp.

Set on an abandoned spaceship 1000 years in the future and peopled with characters and crew right out of the 90's. The set is some industrial complex, like an oil tanker or whatever. They use no ASU so the controls consist racks of old TV equipment. One location is in the crew lunchroom which sports an old TV and VCR as well as a water cooler with a demijohn. The Listerine seems to get the best lighting, mounted on the wall. The dialog is filled with slang that's pretty dated ("uh-uh-oh, Daddy-O") but then maybe that's just the point. The most interesting part of the film is in the cargo hold with the floating coffins a la Hotel Transylvania. The rest of the film is a full-on parody of the Alien and Alien franchise with gags, shameless rip-offs of all the best horror movies and song titles. At one point Casper VanDien even tells his crew to "leave the Alien" with a straight face. The film would have been great if they had just let everyone run with the satire but they keep attempting to make the film serious....maybe the backers were on the influence that day. Anyway, the soundtrack is pretty killer if you're not too picky. FX are pretty good given the sets.

As a fan of horror and gore, I found this movie to be a major letdown. The effects and camera work were impressive, yes, and the humor was well-timed, but... something was missing. First, a large portion of the film is spent exploring nuances of Jack Brooks' character, despite the fact that everything we need to know about his aggression is delivered within seconds of the opening title cards. As such the narration and many of the flashbacks are unnecessary. The pacing of the second act was tedious. Most of it is focused on Freddy Krueger fighting, then running, then fighting some more, then talking with his girlfriend and saying some snappy quips. All the while, the second act is punctuated with several scenes of Jack discussing his rage with his best friend. (Definitely the best scenes of the film, excellent dialog and plenty of laughs.) Then, without warning, Jack decides to kill all the monsters. And then the movie ends. All in all, as a comedic homage to 1980s horror movies, Jack Brooks: Monster Slayer has plenty of potential but is purposeless and plods along like a snail's pace. Hopefully, these issues will be addressed before Jack 2: Stairway to Hell or Jack vs. Dead go into production
